hints: Focus on what happens to the oxidising agent itself, it starts in a high oxidation state with a strong colour and changes as it is reduced.
Recall that acidified dichromate(VI) starts orange due to $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ and forms green $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ when reduced.
Now link the same idea to manganate(VII), purple $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced to almost colourless $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ in acid, so check which row shows both changes correctly.
walkthrough:
**Recall the dichromate colour change**

Think of the classic test for alcohols. Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is a bright orange solution.

Chemical change:
$$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} \text{ (orange)} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} \text{ (green)}$$

**Recall the manganate colour change**

Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is an intense purple solution. In acidic conditions it is reduced all the way to manganese(II).

Chemical change:
$$\text{MnO}_4^- \text{ (purple)} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} \text{ (colourless)}$$

**Match to the table**

So we need orange to green for dichromate, and purple to colourless for manganate. That combination matches only one row, giving the correct deduction.

options.A: This reverses the dichromate change. Green is the colour after reduction to Cr3+, not before. Orange must come first.
options.B: The dichromate part is correct (orange to green) but the manganate part is backwards. Manganate starts purple and becomes colourless, it does not start colourless and turn purple on reduction.
options.C: Correct. Acidified dichromate(VI) changes from orange to green as Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), and acidified manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless as Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(II).
options.D: This swaps the two reagents completely. Purple to colourless belongs to manganate(VII), not dichromate, and orange to green belongs to dichromate, not manganate.
